query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under combined cyclic mechanical loading and corrosive exposure, the high-entropy alloy's resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the in situ formation and dynamic restructuring of a nanoscale passivation film that continuously repairs and adapts to surface damage.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, well-annealed high-entropy alloy (HEA) with minimal pre‐existing surface defects.
generation.intervention: Apply cyclic mechanical loading in a corrosive (e.g., chloride-rich) environment while using in situ advanced characterization (e.g., high‐resolution TEM with an attached electrochemical cell or electrochemical AFM) to monitor surface changes.
generation.conditions: Testing under cyclic stress and in a corrosive medium that emulates harsh operational environments (e.g., high-concentration chlorides or acid) versus control conditions lacking cyclic loading or corrosive exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: The dynamically evolving nanoscale passivation layer that forms and restructures under applied strain.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical strains induce surface restructuring that not only heals micro-damages but also enhances the formation and stability of an oxide/passivating film. This film, in turn, provides a protective barrier against corrosive attack while its adaptive nature reduces wear damage, thereby synergistically enhancing overall durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a matched baseline HEA (or under static exposure conditions), the alloy under cyclic loading will exhibit a denser, more uniform passivation film, leading to lower wear rates and reduced corrosion current densities. The protective film should be directly observable via in situ methods, correlating with improved tribocorrosion performance.
generation.baseline: A control sample of the same HEA subjected either to static (non-cyclic) loading in the same corrosive medium or one lacking the composition that supports dynamic restructuring (e.g., without key alloying elements such as Zr or Mo that promote passivation).
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold under conditions where mechanical loads are sufficiently cyclic to drive restructuring and where the corrosive aggressiveness is moderate enough to allow passivation film formation. It may fail under quasi-static loading or in environments where corrosion proceeds too rapidly for dynamic film healing to occur.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement due to restructuring and the precise interplay between film formation kinetics and wear damage under varying loading frequencies remain to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically processed HEA samples. Subject one set to simultaneous cyclic mechanical loading in a controlled corrosive chloride solution while monitoring the surface in real time with in situ high-resolution TEM or electrochemical AFM. Subject the control set to the same corrosive environment under static conditions. Compare the evolution and characteristics of the surface passivation layer, wear tracks, and corrosion behavior.
measurements: Real-time imaging of passivation film formation and restructuring using in situ TEM or AFM.
Wear rates measured via profilometry or weight loss tests.
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization, EIS) to determine corrosion current density and passivation behavior.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If in situ characterization does not reveal a correlation between cyclic loading and enhanced/dynamic passivation film formation – or if both cyclic and static conditions produce similar film characteristics and wear/corrosion rates – then the hypothesis that dynamic restructuring under cyclic load governs the improved simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of Zr to multielement alloys allows the improvement of some mechanical properties []; thus, in TiMoNbZrx alloy, Zr determined the improvement of wear resistance, due to the formation of an oxide film that acts as a lubricant []. In terms of corrosion resistance, grain refinement plays a great role, and a small addition of Zr can contribute to grain refinement []. Thus, our study focuses on the use of the Mo and Zr in an HEA for the manufacture of mechanical parts used in the geothermal industry at high temperature and in corrosive media. The impact of Zr addition on the CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy’s microstructure, elastic modulus, and corrosion characteristics is examined in this work. In order to analyze the microstructure of the samples with and without Zr, optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) are employed, microhardness tests are performed, a three-point bending test is used to evaluate the modulus of elasticity and linear polarization (LP), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is applied to examine electrochemical responses, corrosion kinetics, and interface parameters.

To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. frame.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with a multi-principal element microstructure engineered for surface integrity, starting from a homogenized, well-annealed state to minimize pre-existing defects.
frame.goal: To establish that the interplay between nanoscale passivation film formation (which offers chemical stability) and dynamic, strain-induced restructuring (which modifies surface mechanical properties) governs simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion in HEAs.
frame.limitation: A unified, single-mechanistic explanation for the synergistic protection against combined wear and corrosion in HEAs remains unestablished.
constraints: controlled comparison with a matched baseline
clear delineation of wear, corrosion, and their combined effects
regime: Exposure to harsh environments combining mechanical wear (e.g., abrasive or erosive conditions under cyclic stresses) with corrosive media (e.g., chloride-rich or acidic solutions)
Testing under cyclic loading to simulate real-world degrading conditions
prior_attempts: Separately benchmarked experiments on wear-only and corrosion-only conditions which did not capture the interactive effects
Previous comparisons to conventional alloys where improved corrosion was obtained at the expense of mechanical wear resistance, thus not providing a holistic understanding

families.best_lever: Use in situ techniques such as high‐resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with an electrochemical cell or in situ electrochemical atomic force microscopy (AFM) during cyclic loading to capture the evolution of the passivation layer and restructuring processes.
